memory_update.text: POWL should remain in the AI data-center electrical-BOP universe as a direct switchgear and packaged electrical-systems supplier; evidence to track is data-center order recurrence, backlog mix, and lead-time/capacity commentary.

MYRG should be tracked as an underfollowed services/interconnection candidate because data-center power constraints can pull demand into electrical construction, substations, and grid-upgrade execution.

IESC is a plausible underfollowed electrical-services/data-center infrastructure candidate, but later layers should verify primary filings because current evidence includes third-party filing summaries.

For this node, the most direct non-megacap public-market mappings appear to be medium-voltage switchgear, packaged electrical systems, electrical construction, substation/interconnection services, and data-center electrical commissioning.

Need a dedicated Layer 1B/1C pass on transformer manufacturers, busbar/cable-management suppliers, testing/commissioning firms, and listed distributors; several may be OTC, foreign-listed, or buried inside larger conglomerates.

POWL is a high-priority direct supplier candidate for AI data-center electrical BOP due to medium-voltage switchgear exposure, record backlog, and explicit data-center order evidence; now above the preferred $300M-$10B range, so treat as a pure-exposure large-cap exception rather than an undiscovered small cap.

MYRG is a mid-cap underfollowed services candidate for grid interconnection, substations, transmission/distribution, and data-center electrical construction; key verification is data-center-specific backlog and margin contribution.

PRIM is a mid-cap underfollowed infrastructure-services candidate with power delivery and acquired data-center services exposure; key verification is whether data-center/power delivery materially changes consolidated revenue and margins.

Need a separate follow-up pass for smaller component suppliers below $10B: conduit, cable tray, busway, enclosures, dry-type transformers, power-quality gear, testing/commissioning, and inspection/certification providers. Current pass found stronger evidence in contractors and switchgear than in obscure listed component makers.
Evidence supports the node hypothesis that AI deployment delays can arise from physical electrical infrastructure constraints even when compute capital and GPU supply are available.

POWL should be carried forward as a direct switchgear/electrical distribution chokepoint candidate; verify the >$400M data-center award, backlog duration, customer concentration, and capacity constraints.

IESC should be carried forward as a data-center electrical/technology systems and infrastructure services candidate; its $3.9B backlog and data-center language make it a high-priority underfollowed services node.
MYRG is a lower-attention electrical construction and grid-services candidate; the exposure is plausible but needs stronger proof of direct AI data-center or large-load interconnection work.

Layer 2 should add a transformer-specific sub-search, because U.S.-listed pure-play transformer candidates are scarce; likely candidates may be foreign-listed, OTC, or embedded inside diversified electrical equipment companies.
The bottleneck appears to be broadening from data-center power/cooling equipment into switchgear, substations, field electrical labor, interconnection engineering, and power-ready site development.

POWL should move to the top of the underfollowed AI-power watchlist because the company disclosed a data-center order exceeding $400 million tied to behind-the-meter on-site generation assets, directly validating electrical balance-of-plant scarcity.

PRIM is a mid-cap utility-services and power-delivery candidate; the key verification path is whether utility backlog and power delivery growth are specifically tied to data-center load growth and interconnection work.

ATKR remains a speculative shadow candidate: data-center applicability is real at the product-description level, but the evidence is not yet strong enough without segment-level revenue or margin linkage.

The AI data-center bottleneck is increasingly visible in electrical orders, switchgear, behind-the-meter generation, utility power delivery, and construction services rather than only in chips or servers.

Need a later Layer 2 pass on transformer manufacturers, busbar suppliers, electrical enclosure vendors, grid interconnection software, commissioning/testing firms, and regional utility exposure near major data-center clusters.
